history.title: Crew Launch Week 6: Feedback Is Information, Not a Verdict

data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Perseverance. "I persevere to produce high quality work."

This week you practice rating your own work against a target before anyone else does, and then using feedback as a map.

1. Read **Feedback Is Information, Not a Verdict** (10 minutes).
2. Learn the **Glossary** words, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Verdict or Map?** chart open.
4. Sort the cards in **Verdict Thinking or Map Thinking?**
5. Take the quiz. Question 4 is about the difference between revising and redoing.
6. Open the SEL Hub and choose [Growth Mindset](#sel-hub/growthmindset?station=sel_station_crew_launch_feedback) to practice the one-word change. Then open [HOWL Tracker](#sel-hub/howlTracker?station=sel_station_crew_launch_feedback) and rate your own perseverance for the past two weeks with one piece of evidence for the rating. If a thought like "I am bad at this" is loud, try [CBT Thought Record](#sel-hub/thoughtRecord?station=sel_station_crew_launch_feedback) on it.
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to self-assess one piece of real work against its rubric.
8. Lock it in with **Remember Gap, Map, Yet**.
9. Finish with the **Explore Challenge: Rate It Before They Do**, on an assignment due this week.

Your commitment: this week, rate one assignment against its rubric before turning it in, and compare your rating to the feedback you get. 🗺

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: Feedback Is Information, Not a Verdict
history.data:
## Feedback Is Information, Not a Verdict

**HOWL: "I persevere to produce high quality work."**

Two Perseverance behaviors in the King **HOWLs** go together: **assess** your work using **targets** and **rubrics**, and learn from **feedback** and **revise**. Both are about the same skill. Looking at your own work honestly, before and after someone else does, and then changing it.

Feedback is hard to hear. When a teacher hands back a draft with comments, a lot of people feel one of two things. Either "this means I am bad at this," or "this teacher just does not like my work." Both feelings are normal. Both are also wrong about what feedback is. Feedback is information about the **gap** between where the work is and where the target is. It is not a **verdict** about you.

That is why targets and rubrics matter. A learning target says what the work is supposed to do. A rubric says what each level of doing it looks like. When you have those in front of you, you can check your own work before anyone else sees it. That is self-assessment. It turns feedback from a surprise into a confirmation. You already knew the **evidence** was thin in paragraph two. The teacher just agreed.

Here is a fictional example. Leila turns in a science explanation. It comes back with three comments: "claim is clear," "evidence is missing for the second part," "reasoning needs to connect the evidence to the claim." Leila's first reaction is a sinking feeling. Then she opens the rubric. The rubric has three rows: claim, evidence, reasoning. She rates her own draft on each row. Claim, level 3. Evidence, level 2. Reasoning, level 2. The teacher's comments and her own ratings match. Now the comments are not a judgment. They are a map. She adds one piece of evidence for the second part and one sentence connecting it to the claim. That is the whole revision. Twenty minutes.

Revising is not **redoing**. Redoing means starting over because the first try felt bad. Revising means keeping what works and changing what the target says to change. Most revisions are small. The people who revise well are not the people with the most talent. They are the people who can look at a rubric row, look at their work, and say "that one, not that one" without it feeling like an attack.

There is a thought that gets in the way: "I cannot do this." The growth-minded version is one word longer: "I cannot do this **yet**." That word is not a slogan. It is a claim about how brains work. Skills are built by doing the hard thing slightly wrong and then adjusting. Feedback is the adjusting part. Skipping it does not protect you. It just stops the building.

This week you practice rating your own work against a rubric before you get feedback, and then treating the feedback as a map. You will use the HOWL Tracker in the SEL Hub to rate your own perseverance the same way: with evidence, not with a feeling.

data.def: Information about the gap between where the work is and where the target is.
A final judgment. Feedback is not one.
What the work is supposed to do, written in words a student can check.
A chart that says what each level of the work looks like, row by row.
To rate work against what it is supposed to do. Doing it to your own work first is the responsible version.
Keep what works, change what the target says to change.
Start over because the first try felt bad. Usually not what the target asks for.
Something in the work you can point to that supports a rating.
The space between the work as it is and the work as the target describes it.
The word that turns "I cannot do this" into a claim about how brains build skills.
A small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to support each other and reflect on learning. EL Education's word for advisory.
Habit of Work and Learning: a way of working that your school teaches and scores separately from academic grades. At King, the three are Respect, Responsibility, and Perseverance.

items.content: "Three comments. I am terrible at science writing."
"Claim row is fine. Evidence row is where the gap is."
"She always marks me down. She just does not like my stuff."
"The rubric says level 3 needs two pieces of evidence. I have one."
"I am going to start the whole thing over."
"I will add one sentence connecting the evidence to the claim and leave the rest."
"I cannot write conclusions yet. What does a level 4 conclusion do that mine does not?"
"I cannot write conclusions. I never could."
"My own rating was a 2 on reasoning. The comment agrees. Not a surprise."
"I got comments, so the grade is going to be bad. Why bother fixing it."

questions.question: According to the reading, what is feedback?
options: A judgment about whether you are good at a subject
Information about the gap between the work and the target
A teacher's opinion about the effort you put in
The grade explained in words instead of a number
questions.correctAnswer: Information about the gap between the work and the target

questions.question: What did opening the rubric do for Leila?
options: It showed her the teacher had made a mistake on one comment
It gave her a higher rating than the teacher had given
It turned the comments from a judgment into a map
It told her to start the explanation over from the beginning
questions.correctAnswer: It turned the comments from a judgment into a map

questions.question: Why does the reading say to self-assess BEFORE getting feedback?
options: So the teacher does not have to write as many comments
So you can argue for a higher grade if the feedback is unfair
So you can skip the feedback if your own rating is high
So feedback becomes a confirmation instead of a surprise
questions.correctAnswer: So feedback becomes a confirmation instead of a surprise

questions.question: What is the difference between revising and redoing?
options: Revising keeps what works and changes what the target says to change
Revising means fixing spelling; redoing means fixing ideas
Redoing is for big assignments and revising is for small ones
There is no real difference; they both mean improving the work
questions.correctAnswer: Revising keeps what works and changes what the target says to change

questions.question: What does the reading say the word "yet" is?
options: A slogan teachers use to make students feel better
A polite way of admitting you cannot do something
A claim about how brains build skills by adjusting
A word to use only after you have already improved
questions.correctAnswer: A claim about how brains build skills by adjusting

questions.question: A teacher writes "evidence is thin" on your draft. Write the map-thinking version of your first thought.
questions.expectedAnswer: Something like: The gap is in the evidence row; the next level needs another piece of evidence, so I will add one and keep the rest.

reflections.text: Think of the last feedback you got (no names). Was your first reaction verdict thinking or map thinking? What would the map version have been?

items.text: The target for this work is ____.
On the ____ row, I rate my work a ____ because I can point to ____.
The row with the biggest gap is ____. The next level looks like ____.
To revise, I will keep ____ and change ____.
When the feedback comes back, I expect it to say ____.
I cannot ____ yet. The adjustment I am making is ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 - Starting | 3 - Getting There | 5 - Crew Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rates with evidence | Rates on feeling | Rates with one thing to point to | Rates every row with something to point to |
| Finds the gap | Says "it is all bad" or "it is fine" | Names one row | Names the row and what the next level looks like |
| Revises, not redoes | Starts over | Changes one thing | Keeps what works and changes only what the target says |

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: What if my self-rating is higher than the teacher's?
data.answer: That is useful. It means you and the rubric are reading a row differently. Ask what the next level looks like on that row. That is the ask move from last week.

data.question: What if the feedback is just a grade with no comments?
data.answer: Use the rubric as the comments. Rate each row yourself and find the gap. Then ask the teacher which row cost the most points.

data.question: Is it okay to feel bad when I get feedback?
data.answer: Yes. The sinking feeling is normal. The skill is what you do in the thirty seconds after it: open the rubric.

data.question: What if I really did do everything on the rubric?
data.answer: Then say so, with evidence. "The rubric says two pieces of evidence and here are mine" is map thinking. Teachers can be wrong about a row too.

data.question: How does this connect to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Perseverance HOWL includes assessing your work using targets and rubrics, and learning from feedback and revising. Rating your own work first and then revising is that HOWL, in two sentences.

cards.target: Feedback is information about the gap, and the rubric turns it into a map
essentialFacts: Feedback is information about the gap between where the work is and where the target is.
It is not a verdict about you.
Now the comments are not a judgment. They are a map.
cards.aiExample: Find the gap, read the map, skip the verdict, close the gap. Say it twice and the rhyme carries the order: gap first, map second, verdict never.
cards.mapping: Gap and map rhyme, which pairs the idea (a gap) with the tool (the rubric map); "skip the verdict" names the thing to leave out; "close the gap" is the revision.
cards.scaffoldStarter: Find the ____, read the ____, skip the ____.
scaffoldSteps: Put them in a line with a beat.
Say it the next time a paper comes back.
coachPrompts: Which of the three words is the one you forget when the feedback stings?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own rhyme or beat for gap, map, verdict.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your rhyme change the first thirty seconds after feedback?

hookFact.text: She adds one piece of evidence for the second part and one sentence connecting it to the claim. That is the whole revision. Twenty minutes.

cards.target: "Yet" turns "I cannot" into a claim about how skills are built
essentialFacts: The growth-minded version is one word longer: "I cannot do this yet."
Skills are built by doing the hard thing slightly wrong and then adjusting.
cards.aiExample: YET = not YET built. A house that is not built yet is still a house that is going to exist. "I cannot do this yet" means the skill is under construction, not cancelled.
cards.mapping: Yet links to a building under construction: something unfinished but in progress, which is what the word claims about a skill.
scaffoldSteps: Write a sentence you have said that starts with "I cannot."
coachPrompts: What is the difference between "I cannot do this yet" and "I will try harder"?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own picture or word link for yet.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your link help you keep going after a low rubric row?

history.title: Explore Challenge: Rate It Before They Do

data.title: Rate It Before They Do
data.instructions: Take one real assignment due this week that has a rubric or a learning target. Rate your own draft row by row with evidence before you turn it in, predict the feedback, then compare your prediction to what comes back and revise.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behaviors are self-assessing with targets and rubrics and learning from feedback to revise. Predicting feedback and checking the prediction makes both behaviors observable and gives the student a result they can compare, not a feeling.

brief.context: You have an assignment due this week with a rubric or a target. Most students turn it in and wait. You are going to rate it first.
brief.role: A student exploring how close their self-assessment is to the teacher's
brief.audience: You. Then your Crew, who hears how close the prediction was and what you revised.
brief.drivingQuestion: How close is my own rubric rating to the feedback I actually get, and which row did I misjudge?
brief.seedDirection: Print or copy the rubric. For each row, write your rating and one thing in the draft you can point to. Write down what you expect the feedback to say. Turn it in. Compare.
lockedLessonFacts: Feedback is information about the gap between where the work is and where the target is; it is not a verdict.
A rubric says what each level of the work looks like, row by row.
Self-assessment turns feedback from a surprise into a confirmation.
Revising means keeping what works and changing what the target says to change.
openQuestions: Which row am I least sure how to rate?
What evidence in my draft supports each rating?
Which row do I predict the teacher will mark lowest?
After the feedback comes back, which row did I misjudge, and why?
stakeholders: The teacher who gives the feedback
Your Crew leader, who can help you read a rubric row
criteria: Every rubric row has a self-rating and one piece of evidence
A written prediction of the feedback exists before turning in
The comparison names at least one row where the prediction matched and one where it did not, or explains why all matched
The revision changes only what the target says to change
Uses at least three glossary words correctly
constraints: Self-rating done before turning in, not after
The record is honest about the misjudged row
brief.deliverable: A rubric with your ratings and evidence, your written prediction, a short comparison to the real feedback, and the revised piece (or the revision plan if the feedback is not back yet).

parallelExample.context: A fictional student rated her history paragraph.
parallelExample.move: She gave herself a 3 on evidence and a 3 on reasoning and predicted the teacher would say the same. The feedback gave evidence a 3 and reasoning a 2, with the comment "you quote the source but do not say why it matters." Her comparison said: "I misjudged reasoning. I thought quoting was reasoning. Next level means saying why." She added two sentences and kept the rest.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows the misjudged row is the most useful result: it tells her exactly which idea she was reading wrong.

supports.frameStarter: On the ____ row I rated myself ____ because ____. I predicted the feedback would say ____.
frameChoices: I misjudged ____, because I thought ____ meant ____.
coachPrompts: If every prediction matched, what does that tell you about your self-assessment? Is the rubric row you are most sure about actually the one you should check hardest?
Which row would you ask the teacher about, using the four moves from last week?

data.coachHint: Some students will not get feedback back within the week. The prediction and the self-rating are still the deliverable; the comparison can come the following Crew.
data.sourceExcerpt: The teacher's comments and her own ratings match. Now the comments are not a judgment. They are a map. She adds one piece of evidence for the second part and one sentence connecting it to the claim. That is the whole revision.
